docs.title: Two-phase aggregation — how groupBy reduces shuffle cost
docs.text:
When you run a groupBy, Spark doesn't shuffle raw rows directly. It runs aggregation in two phases to reduce the volume of data crossing the network.

Think of a national election count. Each constituency counts their own local votes first, then sends only the totals to the central office — not every individual ballot. The central office merges the totals. Far less data travels.

Spark does the same:

Phase 1 (partial): Each executor computes a partial result on its own partition. For a groupBy("ville").avg("Heart_Rate"), each executor finds the local sum and count of Heart_Rate for each city it holds.

Phase 2 (finalmerge): After the shuffle, each executor receives partial results from all other executors for its assigned cities, and merges them into the final answer.

Visible in the physical plan as two GroupingAgg nodes — one with partial_ prefix before the shuffle, one with finalmerge_ prefix after:

PhotonGroupingAgg ... finalmerge_avg(...)    ← Phase 2: merge after shuffle
   +- PhotonShuffleExchangeSource
      +- PhotonShuffleExchangeSink hashpartitioning(ville, 41)
         +- PhotonGroupingAgg ... partial_avg(...)   ← Phase 1: local compute before shuffle

Only the compact partial summaries cross the network — not every row. This is why groupBy is less expensive than it first appears.

docs.title: AQE — Adaptive Query Execution
docs.text:
Spark builds a plan before your job runs, but with AQE enabled it can revise that plan mid-execution based on what it actually sees in the data.

Think of a GPS that recalculates based on live traffic rather than only predicted traffic. The initial route was sensible — but once you're driving and real conditions are visible, it adjusts.

The most visible effect of AQE is shuffle partition count. The default is 200, but AQE measures the actual data volume after the shuffle write and picks a more appropriate number. A small dataset might get 8 or 41 partitions instead of 200 — fewer tasks, less overhead.

Visible in the physical plan as:

AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false

isFinalPlan=false means the plan is still the initial version — AQE hasn't finished optimising. By the time the job completes, the plan may have changed. isFinalPlan=true means AQE has locked in its final decisions.

AQE is enabled by default on Databricks. You don't configure it — it works automatically.

docs.title: 1. Broadcast join — eliminate the shuffle entirely
docs.text:
When one side of a join is small (a few hundred rows to a few hundred MB), broadcast it. Spark sends a full copy to every executor — no shuffle needed.

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

# Without broadcast — both tables shuffle
df_result = df_transactions.join(df_state_codes, "state_code", "left")

# With broadcast — df_state_codes goes to every executor, no shuffle
df_result = df_transactions.join(broadcast(df_state_codes), "state_code", "left")

Real example: 10 crore transaction rows joined to a 500-row state codes table. Without broadcast, both tables shuffle — that's 10 crore rows moving across the network. With broadcast, the 500 rows get copied to every executor, and only the large table moves (to its own executors for processing). The 500-row copy is negligible.

The broadcast size limit

The broadcast table has to fit in memory on every executor simultaneously. If it's too large, the executor runs out of memory and the job fails.

Spark controls this with a threshold setting:

spark.conf.get("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold")  # default: 10MB

Below this threshold, Spark automatically broadcasts the small table even without you explicitly calling broadcast(). Above it, Spark falls back to a regular shuffle join. You can tune this:

# Allow broadcast for tables up to 100MB
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "104857600")

# Disable auto-broadcast entirely
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1")

Rule of thumb: broadcast is safe up to ~200MB per executor. Beyond that, use a shuffle join. A few hundred rows to a few thousand rows is always safe.

docs.title: 2. Filter before you shuffle
docs.text:
The less data going into a shuffle, the cheaper it is. Push filters as early as possible — before any groupBy or join.

# Worse — shuffle happens on all rows, then filter
df.groupBy("city").count().filter(col("city") == "Mumbai")

# Better — filter first, then shuffle only Mumbai rows
df.filter(col("city") == "Mumbai").groupBy("city").count()

Spark's optimizer often does this automatically (predicate pushdown), but being explicit never hurts.

docs.title: 3. Avoid unnecessary wide operations
docs.text:
orderBy() is a full global sort — one of the most expensive operations. If you only need the top N rows, use limit() after ordering, or better, use a window function. If you don't need a global sort at all, don't add one.

distinct() on a large DataFrame is expensive. If you know duplicates are rare, question whether you need it.

docs.title: Shuffle and the physical plan — the connection
docs.text:
Your class notes made this connection:

explain command → groupBy → Exchange (shuffle)

Now the full picture:

flowchart LR
    A["df.groupBy('city').count()"] -->|"wide transformation"| B["Shuffle triggered"]
    B -->|"visible as"| C["Exchange in explain()"]
    B -->|"visible as"| D["Shuffle Read/Write\nin Spark UI"]
    B -->|"cost"| E["Disk write + Network + Disk read"]

groupBy is a wide transformation → triggers a shuffle → Exchange appears in the physical plan → you see shuffle read/write metrics in the Spark UI. All four are describing the same thing at different levels.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept One line Shuffle Data moving across the network between executors — caused by wide transformations What causes it groupBy, join (non-broadcast), orderBy, distinct, repartition What doesn't filter, select, withColumn, coalesce Three costs Disk write → network transfer → disk read How to spot it Exchange in explain(), shuffle read/write in Spark UI How to reduce it Broadcast join, filter early, avoid unnecessary orderBy/distinct Shuffle partitions Default 200 — reduce for small clusters (spark.sql.shuffle.partitions) Two-phase aggregation groupBy computes partial results locally before shuffling — reduces data crossing the network AQE Adaptive Query Execution — Spark revises the plan mid-run based on actual data; auto-tunes shuffle partitions

docs.title: The one idea everything else builds on
docs.text:
Think about counting votes in a general election. One person counting 90 crore votes would take forever. So instead you have counting centers across every constituency — each center handles its local votes, and the final tally gets combined at the end.

That's distributed computing. Instead of one powerful machine doing all the work sequentially, you split the data across many machines, process in parallel, and combine the results. Spark is the engine that manages this entire operation.

docs.title: Spark Engine → Compute Engine
docs.text:
Spark is not a database. It does not store data. It is a compute engine — its only job is to process data that lives somewhere else (a data lake, cloud storage, Delta tables) and return results.

Database (e.g. SQL Server) Spark Stores data? Yes No Processes data? Yes Yes Where data lives On the same server External storage (ADLS, S3, OneLake) Scales how? Bigger server More machines in the cluster

When you run a PySpark notebook on Databricks, you're not running code on your laptop. You're sending instructions to a Spark engine running on a cluster of machines in the cloud. Spark reads from storage, processes, and writes back to storage.

docs.title: Classic Compute vs Serverless Compute
docs.text: There are two ways Spark compute is provisioned in Databricks.

docs.title: Classic Compute (Cluster you control)
docs.text:
You create a cluster manually. You choose how many machines, how much RAM, which Spark version. The cluster starts up (takes 3–5 minutes), runs until you stop it or it auto-terminates, and you're billed for every minute it's alive — whether it's actively processing data or sitting idle.

Think of it like renting an office. The office is yours from 9am to 6pm regardless of whether your team is working or not.

flowchart LR
    A[You create cluster] --> B[Cluster running]
    B --> C["You pay\n(idle or active)"]

You control: - Number of workers - Machine type (memory/CPU) - Auto-scaling rules - Databricks Runtime version

Use Classic when: - You need specific cluster configurations - You're running long, continuous jobs - You need to install custom libraries on the cluster

docs.title: Serverless Compute
docs.text:
No cluster to configure. You write your notebook, hit run, and Databricks figures out the compute. Behind the scenes it spins up resources, runs your code, and tears everything down when done. You pay only for the time your code is actually executing.

flowchart LR
    A[You run code] --> B[Databricks manages everything]
    B --> C["You pay\n(execution time only)"]

Databricks manages: - Provisioning machines - Scaling up and down - Cluster configuration - Teardown after job completes

Use Serverless when: - You want zero cluster management - You run intermittent jobs (not continuous) - You're on a cost-sensitive setup (no idle billing) - You're on Databricks Free Edition or a trial

The trade-off: serverless gives you less control over configuration. For learning and most standard pipelines, serverless is the better default.

docs.title: What is a Cluster?
docs.text:
A cluster is a group of machines that work together as one unit. When you submit a Spark job, it runs on the cluster.

Every cluster has two types of machines:

graph TD
    D["🖥️ Driver Node\n(coordinates everything)"]
    W1["⚙️ Worker Node 1\nTask 1"]
    W2["⚙️ Worker Node 2\nTask 2"]
    W3["⚙️ Worker Node 3\nTask 3"]
    D --> W1
    D --> W2
    D --> W3

docs.title: Driver Node — the Tech Lead
docs.text:
The Driver is the coordinator. There is exactly one Driver per cluster. It:

  • Receives your code (the PySpark instructions you write)
  • Builds an execution plan (decides how to break the job into tasks)
  • Assigns tasks to Worker nodes
  • Monitors progress
  • Collects and assembles the final result

The Driver does not process your data. It manages the workers who do.

If your class used the Tech Lead analogy — that's exactly right. The Tech Lead reads the requirements, breaks the work into tickets, assigns them to developers, reviews what comes back, and produces the final output. The Tech Lead doesn't write every line of code.

# When you call .collect() or .show(), the Driver is what gets the result
# The heavy lifting happened on the workers
df.show()  # Driver asked workers → workers sent results back → Driver displays it

What lives on the Driver: - Your PySpark application code - The execution plan (DAG) - Metadata and aggregated results

What does NOT live on the Driver: - Your actual data (that's distributed across workers)

docs.title: Worker Nodes — the development team
docs.text:
Workers are the machines in the cluster. A cluster can have 2, 10, or 100+ workers depending on the workload. Each worker:

  • Gets assigned a subset of the data (called a partition)
  • Reads files from storage
  • Runs transformations on its partition
  • Writes output directly to storage (Delta table, parquet, etc.)
  • Works in parallel with all other workers
  • Sends results or metadata back to the Driver when done

Using the class analogy: the Driver (Tech Lead) gives each Worker (developer) a specific ticket to handle. The developer does their work independently and reports back. No worker waits for another worker to finish before starting.

One important point on "Write Output": when your job writes a Delta table or parquet file, the Executors write directly to storage in parallel — they don't send data back to the Driver first. The Driver only receives a success/failure confirmation, not the actual data. This is what makes large writes fast.

docs.title: Executor — the process that actually runs your code
docs.text:
There are two things on every worker machine, and it's worth being precise about both.

  • Worker Node — the physical machine. It provides CPU, RAM, disk, and network. It knows nothing about Spark.
  • Executor — a Spark process that runs on the worker node. This is what reads partitions, runs tasks, and sends results back to the Driver.

The Worker Node is the office building. The Executor is the employee working inside it. The building provides space and power — the employee does the work.

Worker Node (the machine)
└── Executor (Spark process)
    ├── Task 1 → processes partition 1
    ├── Task 2 → processes partition 2
    └── Task 3 → processes partition 3

Each executor can run multiple tasks simultaneously — one per CPU core. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks in parallel.

Executors: - Hold data in memory while processing - Write to disk if memory runs out (spill) - Send results back to the Driver when done

In the Spark UI and in error logs, "executor" appears constantly. Now you know exactly what it refers to.

docs.title: Core, Parallelism, and MPP
docs.text:
A core is a CPU slot on an executor. One core runs one task at a time.

If an executor has 4 cores, it runs 4 tasks simultaneously. 10 executors × 4 cores = 40 tasks running in parallel across the cluster.

10 executors × 4 cores = 40 parallel tasks
200 partitions ÷ 40 cores = 5 waves to complete the job

This is what Massively Parallel Processing (MPP) means in practice. Large data gets split into many partitions. Each partition becomes a task. Tasks run simultaneously across all available cores. More cores = faster job.

Term What it means Core One CPU slot — runs one task at a time Parallelism Number of tasks running simultaneously across all cores MPP Processing large data by splitting into partitions and running them in parallel

The cluster sizing question — "how many workers do I need?" — comes down to: how many cores do I need running in parallel to finish this job in an acceptable time?

docs.title: How Executors and the Driver communicate
docs.text:
The Driver doesn't just hand out tasks and forget. There's constant back-and-forth:

  • Driver assigns tasks to Executors
  • Executors send status updates back to the Driver as tasks run
  • When a task completes, the Executor sends results back to the Driver
  • If a task fails, the Executor reports the failure — the Driver decides whether to retry
flowchart LR
    D["Driver"] -->|"assigns tasks"| E["Executors"]
    E -->|"status updates + results"| D
    E -->|"task failure"| D
    D -->|"retry or abort"| E

This communication happens over the network. It's also why the Driver should never do heavy computation itself — it's too busy coordinating.

docs.title: How tasks get distributed
docs.text:
When you run a Spark operation on a large DataFrame, Spark doesn't process the entire dataset in one go. It splits the data into partitions — chunks of rows. Each partition becomes a task, and each task goes to a worker.

flowchart TD
    A["100 crore rows of transaction data"]
    B["Split into 200 partitions\n(5 lakh rows each)"]
    C["200 tasks distributed to workers"]
    D["10 workers run in parallel\n(each handles 20 tasks)"]
    E["Driver assembles final result"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E

You never write this split logic yourself — Spark handles it automatically. This is why PySpark is fast on large data: the work runs in parallel across all workers instead of sequentially on one machine.

docs.title: Task Scheduling — how tasks run in waves
docs.text:
When a Job has more tasks than available cores, Spark doesn't wait for everything to be ready. It schedules in waves — the first batch fills all available cores, and as each task completes, the next one is immediately assigned.

flowchart TD
    A["200 tasks · 40 cores available"]
    B["Wave 1: tasks 1–40 run simultaneously"]
    C["Wave 2: tasks 41–80 run"]
    D["Wave 3: tasks 81–120 run"]
    E["... continues until all 200 tasks done"]
    F["Driver assembles final result"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F

This is why adding more cores (bigger cluster) speeds up a job — each wave processes more tasks, so fewer waves are needed to finish.

The Driver manages this scheduling. It tracks which executors are free and assigns the next task as soon as a core becomes available. You can see each wave in the Spark UI as a set of tasks running at the same time.

docs.title: Scale Up vs Scale Down
docs.text:
A cluster can adjust the number of workers based on load.

What happens When Scale up More workers are added to the cluster Job is complex, queue of tasks is building up Scale down Workers are removed when they're idle Job is finished or lighter, no point paying for idle machines

In Classic Compute, you configure auto-scaling rules (min workers, max workers). In Serverless, Databricks handles all of this automatically — you don't set anything.

flowchart LR
    A[Heavy job arrives] --> B["Workers added\n(scale up)"]
    C[Job completes] --> D["Idle workers removed\n(scale down)"]
    D --> E["Serverless: cluster\nterminates entirely"]

docs.title: Putting it all together
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["📓 Your PySpark code\n(notebook)"]
    B["🖥️ Driver Node\nparses code · builds plan · assigns tasks"]
    W1["⚙️ Worker 1\npartition 1–20"]
    W2["⚙️ Worker 2\npartition 21–40"]
    W3["⚙️ Worker 3\npartition 41–60"]
    R["🖥️ Driver assembles results"]
    S["💾 Output written to storage\n(Delta table, file, etc.)"]
    A --> B
    B --> W1 & W2 & W3
    W1 & W2 & W3 --> R
    R --> S

This is why PySpark code looks so different from regular Python. You're not writing instructions for one machine running top to bottom. You're writing a plan that Spark will execute in parallel across many machines, with the Driver coordinating everything.

docs.title: Tungsten Engine — how standard Spark manages memory
docs.text:
Before Photon existed, Apache Spark used the Tungsten execution engine to handle memory and CPU efficiency on the JVM.

The JVM manages memory through a process called garbage collection (GC). Periodically, the JVM stops all processing, scans everything in memory, frees what's no longer needed, and then resumes. This is called a GC pause. On a cluster processing large data, these pauses can be seconds long — your job is running, then everything freezes, then it resumes.

Tungsten was Spark's answer to this. It manages memory directly outside the JVM heap — called off-heap memory — in a region the GC never touches. No GC involvement means no GC pauses.

JVM Heap (on-heap)        Off-heap memory
├── your code             ├── Tungsten data storage
├── JVM objects           ├── shuffle buffers
└── GC tracks all of it   └── GC never sees this

Tungsten also generates optimised bytecode at runtime for specific queries rather than using generic interpreted code — faster CPU execution.

Understanding Tungsten matters because off-heap memory is still bounded. When you broadcast a table to every executor, that copy sits in memory. If the table is too large, the executor runs out of memory and the job fails — not slows, fails.

docs.title: Photon Engine — Databricks' native execution layer
docs.text:
When you open the Spark UI or look at a physical plan in Databricks, you'll see references to Photon. This is Databricks' own query engine that sits underneath your PySpark code.

Standard Apache Spark runs on the JVM and uses Tungsten for memory management. Photon goes further — it is rewritten entirely in C++, which manages memory directly at the OS level with no JVM involved at all. It processes data in column-batches rather than row by row.

Your PySpark code
      ↓
Databricks Runtime
      ↓
Photon Engine (C++)   ← replaces standard Spark JVM execution
      ↓
Results

What this means for you:

  • You write nothing differently — same PySpark code, same DataFrame API
  • Photon runs automatically when available. No configuration needed.
  • In the Spark UI, operations show as "Photon" or fall back to standard Spark labels — you can see per-operation which engine ran it
  • Not every operation uses Photon — Python UDFs and some streaming operations fall back to standard Spark

Photon vs Tungsten:

Tungsten Photon Language JVM (Java/Scala) C++ Memory Off-heap via Unsafe API Direct OS memory GC pauses Eliminated via off-heap No JVM — no GC at all Processing Row-based Columnar batches Where Standard Apache Spark Databricks only

On Databricks with Photon enabled, Photon replaces Tungsten's execution. The off-heap memory concern still applies — executor memory is still finite — but Photon handles it more efficiently than Tungsten did.

Why it matters:

If you're comparing job times between Databricks and another Spark environment, Photon is part of why Databricks is faster. It's not a Spark improvement — it's a Databricks layer on top.

Available on Databricks Runtime 9.1+ including Free Edition on compatible cluster types.

docs.title: Classic vs Serverless — quick reference
docs.text: Classic Compute Serverless Compute Cluster setup Manual Automatic Startup time 3–5 minutes Near-instant Scaling Configure auto-scale rules Automatic Idle billing Yes — cluster runs until stopped No — pay only when executing Config control Full control Limited Best for Custom configs, long-running jobs Standard pipelines, learning, cost efficiency Who manages infra You Databricks

docs.title: Before you write a single line of PySpark
docs.text:
Every PySpark program starts the same way:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("MyApp").getOrCreate()

This one line creates the SparkSession. Until you do this, Spark doesn't exist in your program. No connection to the cluster, no ability to read data, no ability to run anything.

Think of it like switching on your laptop before you can open any files. The laptop is the cluster — always there. SparkSession is the power button that connects your code to it.

spark is the variable name by convention. Every DataFrame operation you write — spark.read, spark.sql, df.filter — flows through this object.

In Databricks, the session is created for you automatically. You don't need to write this line in a notebook. It's already running as spark. If you ever see it in someone else's code, now you know what it is.

docs.title: SparkContext — what's inside SparkSession
docs.text:
You'll see SparkContext in error messages and older code. It's the lower-level object that SparkSession wraps internally.

# SparkSession is what you use
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("MyApp").getOrCreate()

# SparkContext is what's inside it — accessible if you need it
sc = spark.sparkContext

SparkContext was the original entry point before Spark 2.0. SparkSession replaced it as a single unified entry point covering DataFrames, SQL, and streaming. You don't create a SparkContext yourself anymore — SparkSession handles that for you.

When you see errors like SparkContext already stopped or Cannot run multiple SparkContexts, it means the underlying context was shut down or a duplicate was attempted. In Databricks this rarely happens, but knowing what SparkContext is makes those errors readable.

docs.title: Why nothing runs when you write a transformation
docs.text:
Write this in a notebook:

df = spark.read.parquet("/data/transactions")
df_filtered = df.filter(df.amount > 1000)
df_grouped = df_filtered.groupBy("city").count()

Run it. Nothing happens. No data was read. No filtering ran. No grouping ran.

That's lazy evaluation.

Spark doesn't execute anything when you write transformations. It just builds a plan — a list of "here's what I want to do". The plan stays as a plan until you ask for a result.

The grocery list analogy: you can write 50 items on a list — rice, dal, vegetables, snacks — and it costs you nothing. No time, no effort. The work only happens when you go to the shop. In Spark, writing transformations is making the list. Calling an action is going to the shop.

flowchart TD
    A["df = spark.read.parquet(...)"] -->|"adds to plan"| B["df.filter(df.amount > 1000)"]
    B -->|"adds to plan"| C["df.groupBy('city').count()"]
    C -->|"plan complete — nothing has run yet"| D{"Action called?"}
    D -->|"No"| E["Plan sits idle"]
    D -->|"Yes — .show()"| F["Spark executes the full plan"]
    F --> G["Results returned"]

Why does Spark do this? Because it can look at the whole plan and optimise before running anything. If you filter early and join late, Spark might reorder operations to be more efficient. It can only do that if it sees the full picture first.

docs.title: Transformations vs Actions
docs.text: Every operation in PySpark is one of two things.

docs.title: How to tell which is which
docs.text:
Rule 1 — what does it return?

  • Returns a DataFrame → Transformation
  • Returns a Python value (number, list, row) or writes to storage → Action

Rule 2 — the chain test:

Can you put another .filter() after it?

df.filter(...).filter(...)   # works — both transformations, both return DataFrames
df.count().filter(...)       # fails — count() returns an int, not a DataFrame

If you can chain it, it's a transformation. If the result is something you'd print or save, it's an action.

docs.title: Transformations — narrow (no data movement)
docs.text:
These stay within each partition. Fast, no network cost.

Operation What it does .filter() / .where() Keep rows that match a condition .select() Choose which columns to keep .withColumn() Add or modify a column .withColumnRenamed() Rename a column .drop() Remove a column .cast() Change a column's data type .alias() Give a column or DataFrame a new name .limit(n) Keep only the first n rows .na.fill() Replace nulls with a value .na.drop() Drop rows containing nulls .dropna() Same as na.drop() .fillna() Same as na.fill() .coalesce(n) Reduce partition count without a shuffle .union() / .unionByName() Stack two DataFrames vertically

docs.title: Transformations — wide (causes a shuffle)
docs.text:
These require data to move across partitions. Slower — use sparingly.

Operation What it does .groupBy() Group rows by one or more columns .agg() Aggregate after groupBy (sum, avg, max, etc.) .orderBy() / .sort() Sort all rows — requires global shuffle .join() Join two DataFrames (non-broadcast) .distinct() Remove duplicate rows — requires shuffle .dropDuplicates() Remove duplicates by specific columns .repartition(n) Redistribute data into n partitions — always shuffles .pivot() Pivot a column into multiple columns .crossJoin() Cartesian join — every row × every row

docs.title: Actions — trigger execution
docs.text:
These run the plan and return a result. Each one creates a new Job.

Operation Returns What it does .show(n) Nothing (prints) Prints first n rows to screen (default 20) .count() Integer Total number of rows .collect() List of Rows Pulls all data to the Driver — careful on large tables .take(n) List of Rows Returns first n rows as a Python list .first() Single Row Returns the very first row .head(n) List of Rows Same as take(n) .toPandas() Pandas DataFrame Converts to pandas — pulls all data to Driver .write.parquet() Nothing Writes to parquet files .write.csv() Nothing Writes to CSV files .write.format().save() Nothing Writes to any format (Delta, JSON, etc.) .saveAsTable() Nothing Saves as a Delta table in the catalog .explain() Nothing (prints) Prints the physical execution plan

docs.title: Edge cases worth knowing
docs.text:
.limit(n) looks like it should run immediately (you're asking for specific rows), but it's a transformation — it returns a DataFrame and nothing executes until an action is called.

.coalesce(n) — see the dedicated section below for full details and the Databricks Free Edition use case.

.cache() / .persist() — neither a transformation nor an action. It marks the DataFrame for caching, but the cache only fills when an action runs. Nothing happens at the point you call .cache().

.distinct() is wide (causes a shuffle) even though it doesn't feel like it should. To find duplicates across 200 partitions, Spark has to shuffle all rows to compare them globally.

df_filtered = df.filter(df.amount > 1000)   # transformation — plan updated, nothing runs
df_filtered.show()                            # action — plan executes NOW

row_count = df_filtered.count()              # action — returns an int
print(row_count)                             # 42381

docs.title: Controlling partitions with coalesce
docs.text:
One thing that often isn't obvious: each partition becomes a separate output file when you write data.

df_result.write.parquet("/output/transactions")

If the DataFrame has 200 partitions, that write creates 200 parquet files. On Databricks Free Edition with limited workers, this is excessive — tiny files, hard to inspect, and harder to reason about.

coalesce(n) reduces the number of partitions before writing, without causing a shuffle.

# Check current partition count
print(df_result.rdd.getNumPartitions())   # e.g. 8

# Coalesce to 2 partitions before writing → creates 2 output files
df_result.coalesce(2).write.parquet("/output/transactions")

# Coalesce to 1 → single clean output file, easiest to inspect
df_result.coalesce(1).write.parquet("/output/transactions")

docs.title: Why it doesn't shuffle
docs.text:
coalesce merges adjacent partitions on the same worker. Partition 1 and Partition 2 sitting on Worker A get combined into one — no data crosses the network. That's what makes it a narrow transformation.

repartition(n) does the opposite — it redistributes data evenly across n partitions via a full shuffle. Slower, but gives you balanced partition sizes.

coalesce(n) repartition(n) Shuffles? No Yes — full network redistribution Can increase partitions? No Yes Partition balance Uneven (merges nearby) Even (redistributes globally) Use when Reducing for output Rebalancing for better parallelism

docs.title: Why production pipelines use coalesce before writes
docs.text: Spark decides partition count to maximise compute parallelism — more partitions means more tasks running in parallel, which is the right call during processing. But when you write output, each partition becomes a file. 200 shuffle partitions means 200 output files — tiny files that are slow to read downstream, expensive on cloud storage (more API calls per read), and hard to work with. In production pipelines, coalesce before a write is standard practice specifically to control output file count. The partition count that was right for compute is often wrong for storage.

docs.title: The Databricks Free Edition use case
docs.text:
In Free Edition with limited workers, your trainer explicitly used coalesce to demonstrate distributed computing — making it visible how many partitions exist and which worker handles which chunk.

# Read data — Spark decides partition count automatically
df_transactions = spark.read.parquet("/data/transactions")
print(f"Partitions after read: {df_transactions.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")

# Explicitly set partitions to match your worker count
df_result = df_transactions \
    .filter(df_transactions.amount > 1000) \
    .coalesce(2)   # 2 workers in Free Edition → 2 partitions

print(f"Partitions after coalesce: {df_result.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")  # 2

# Each worker now writes one file
df_result.write.parquet("/output/filtered_transactions")

flowchart LR
    A["DataFrame\n200 partitions"] -->|"coalesce(2)"| B["2 partitions"]
    B --> W1["Worker 1\nwrites partition 1\n→ file 1"]
    B --> W2["Worker 2\nwrites partition 2\n→ file 2"]

The partition count directly controls the number of output files. coalesce(2) on 2 workers means each worker writes exactly one file — clean, predictable, and easy to see how work is divided across the cluster.

One practical thing to know: every .count() and every .show() triggers a full execution of everything upstream. If you call .count() three times on the same DataFrame, Spark runs the full plan three times. If you need to reuse a result, cache it — but that's a performance topic for later.

docs.title: Narrow vs Wide Transformations
docs.text: Not all transformations are equal. There are two types, and the difference determines whether your job is fast or slow.

docs.title: Narrow transformation
docs.text:
Every row in the output comes from exactly one partition. No data needs to move across the network. Each partition is processed independently.

Think of it like marking exam papers. You have 100 papers split across 10 tables — 10 papers per table. Each person marks their own 10 papers. No paper moves between tables. That's a narrow transformation.

Examples: filter, select, withColumn, drop

# Narrow — each partition processed independently, no data movement
df.filter(df.amount > 1000)
df.select("city", "amount")
df.withColumn("tax", df.amount * 0.18)

docs.title: Wide transformation
docs.text:
Output rows may need data from multiple partitions. Spark has to redistribute data across the network before it can produce the result. This redistribution is called a shuffle.

Same exam analogy — now you need to sort all 100 papers by subject. Science papers, maths papers, and history papers are mixed across all 10 tables. To group them, papers have to physically move between tables. That movement is the shuffle.

Examples: groupBy, join (non-broadcast), orderBy, distinct

# Wide — rows from all partitions must be redistributed to group by city
df.groupBy("city").count()

# Wide — rows from both DataFrames need to find their match across the cluster
df.join(df2, "id", "left")

graph LR
    subgraph Narrow["Narrow — stays in partition"]
        P1A["Partition 1\nfilter → stays here"]
        P2A["Partition 2\nfilter → stays here"]
        P3A["Partition 3\nfilter → stays here"]
    end
    subgraph Wide["Wide — data moves between partitions"]
        P1B["Partition 1\nsome rows move →"]
        P2B["Partition 2\nsome rows move →"]
        P3B["Partition 3\nsome rows move →"]
        OUT["Regrouped\nresult partitions"]
        P1B & P2B & P3B --> OUT
    end

The shuffle is the expensive part. Moving data across the network takes time — much more than processing it in place. This is exactly why broadcast join exists: by sending the small table to every partition, you avoid the shuffle entirely.

Shuffle is a big enough concept that it has its own detailed page coming — covering what it costs, how to spot it, and how to reduce it.

docs.title: The explain() command — reading the physical plan
docs.text:
Before Spark runs anything, it builds a physical plan — the exact steps it will take to execute your query. You can see this plan by calling .explain().

df.groupBy("city").count().explain()

Output (simplified): 

== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan
+- HashAggregate
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(city)   ← this is the shuffle
      +- Scan parquet

The Exchange step is the shuffle. Whenever you see Exchange in the physical plan, data is moving across the network between partitions.

This is the connection from your class notes: physical plan → groupBy → shuffle. groupBy is a wide transformation, which forces a shuffle (Exchange), which you can see in the plan.

# Narrow — no Exchange in the plan
df.filter(df.amount > 1000).explain()

# Wide — Exchange appears because data must be redistributed
df.groupBy("city").count().explain()

.explain() is your first debugging tool when a job runs slow. If you see more Exchange steps than expected, you have more shuffles than needed — and that's where the time is going.

docs.title: What the optimizer does automatically
docs.text: Before running anything, Spark's Catalyst optimizer looks at your plan and applies transformations to make it faster. Two of the most impactful are visible in every physical plan.

docs.title: Predicate pushdown
docs.text:
A predicate is a filter condition — ville = Paris, Heart_Rate > 100, status = active. Spark pushes these as close to the data source as possible — ideally into the file scan itself.

Think of it like searching for a specific file in a cabinet. Instead of pulling every file out and reading each one, you read the folder labels first and only pull the relevant folder. The irrelevant files never leave the cabinet.

Without predicate pushdown: all rows load into memory, filter runs after. With predicate pushdown: the data source is told to return only matching rows. Non-matching rows never enter memory.

Visible in the physical plan as PushedFilters on the FileScan node:

FileScan csv [...] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(ville), EqualTo(ville,Paris)]

When PushedFilters is empty, there was no filter to push — or the source format doesn't support it.

Note that Spark also automatically adds IsNotNull alongside your filter — it won't attempt to match null values against a string condition.

docs.title: Column pruning
docs.text:
The column equivalent of predicate pushdown. If your query only needs ville and Heart_Rate, Spark reads only those two columns at the source — even if the file has 20 others. The unused columns never enter memory.

Visible in the FileScan node — it only lists the columns it actually needs:

FileScan csv [ville#13186, Heart_Rate#13187]

Both optimisations happen automatically. You write the query clearly — the optimizer handles reducing the data volume before any processing begins.

docs.title: What is a Job?
docs.text:
Every time an action fires, Spark creates a Job.

One action = one Job. Three .show() calls in your notebook = three Jobs.

Each Job is broken down further into Stages and Tasks:

flowchart TD
    A["Action triggered\n(e.g. df.show())"] --> B["Spark creates a Job"]
    B --> C["Job split into Stages\n(based on shuffle boundaries)"]
    C --> D["Each Stage split into Tasks\n(one Task per partition)"]
    D --> E["Tasks distributed to Executors"]
    E --> F["Results returned to Driver"]

You can see all of this in the Spark UI — every Job, every Stage, every Task, how long each one took. When a job is slow, the UI tells you exactly where the time went.

For now, the key point: an action creates a Job. Jobs are what Spark actually runs on the cluster.

docs.title: Why Spark is fast — and when it isn't
In-memory processing
docs.text:
Spark keeps data in RAM as much as possible. RAM is many times faster than reading from disk. A filter on 10 crore rows that runs in memory completes in seconds. The same filter reading from disk every time would take minutes.

This is the core reason Spark is fast on large data — it minimises disk reads by holding intermediate results in memory across operations.

docs.title: Spill to disk
docs.text:
If the data doesn't fit in RAM — because a partition is too large, or the executor doesn't have enough memory — Spark writes the overflow to local disk on the worker node. It processes from disk, then cleans up.

Spill doesn't crash your job. It just slows it down. You'll see it in the Spark UI as "spill (memory)" and "spill (disk)" in the task details.

flowchart LR
    A["Data partition arrives\nat Executor"] --> B{"Fits in RAM?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Processed in memory\nFast"]
    B -->|"No"| D["Spills to disk\nSlow but safe"]
    C --> E["Results sent to Driver"]
    D --> E

When you see a job that runs slowly despite having enough workers, spill is a common reason. The fix is either increasing executor memory or reducing partition size — both are tuning topics.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept One line SparkSession The connection between your code and the cluster — must exist before anything runs SparkContext The lower-level object inside SparkSession — you don't create it directly Lazy evaluation Transformations build a plan; nothing executes until an action is called Transformation Returns a DataFrame — filter, select, join, withColumn — adds to the plan Action Produces a result or writes output — show, count, collect, write — triggers execution Narrow transformation Stays within one partition — no data movement, fast (filter, select, withColumn) Wide transformation Data moves across partitions — causes a shuffle, slower (groupBy, join, orderBy) Shuffle Network movement of data between partitions caused by wide transformations explain() Shows the physical plan — look for Exchange to find shuffles explain(True) Shows all three stages: unresolved logical, optimised logical, physical Predicate pushdown Optimizer pushes filters to the data source — non-matching rows never enter memory Column pruning Optimizer drops unused columns at read time — only needed columns are loaded coalesce(n) Reduces partition count without shuffling — controls number of output files repartition(n) Redistributes data evenly into n partitions — causes a shuffle Job Created when an action fires — one action = one Job In-memory processing Spark holds data in RAM for speed Spill to disk When RAM runs out — job slows down but doesn't fail

docs.title: Think of it like a filing cabinet
docs.text:
Imagine a big filing cabinet at work.

  • Cabinet = the Catalog
  • Each drawer = a Schema
  • Each folder inside a drawer = a Table or a Volume (for raw files)

In Databricks, this is the Unity Catalog. It's the organised structure for storing all your data and files.

Catalog  (the whole cabinet)
  └── Schema  (one drawer)
        └── Tables, Views, Volumes  (folders inside that drawer)

docs.title: How you reference things
docs.text:
Always three parts, dot-separated:

catalog.schema.table_name

Example from Green Grid: 

workspace.green_grid_case_study.Silver_SmartBill

Read that as: "In the workspace cabinet, open the green_grid_case_study drawer, find the Silver_SmartBill folder."

docs.title: What is a Volume?
docs.text:
A Volume is a folder for raw files — CSVs, JSONs, Excel files, etc. It is not a table. You can't query it with SQL. It's just file storage, same as the Files section in a Fabric Lakehouse.

workspace
  └── green_grid_case_study
        └── raw_files  ← this is the Volume (a folder)
              ├── customer_pii.csv
              ├── meter_readings.json
              └── pricing_plans.csv

To read a file from a Volume, you use its path: 

/Volumes/workspace/green_grid_case_study/raw_files/customer_pii.csv

Same structure as the catalog hierarchy. Same logic as a file path on your laptop.

docs.title: Managed vs External Volume
docs.text:
Managed External Where files live Databricks looks after it Your own storage (ADLS, S3) When to use Learning, most projects Production when you control the storage

In the bootcamp we use managed. Databricks handles everything, you just upload files and use them.

docs.title: If you know Microsoft Fabric
docs.text:
Databricks Microsoft Fabric Catalog Workspace Schema Lakehouse Volume Files section in Lakehouse Managed Table Delta Table

Same idea, different names.

docs.title: Three commands you'll use constantly
docs.text:
# Read a file from a volume
spark.read.csv("/Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/file.csv")

# Write data as a table
df.write.saveAsTable("catalog.schema.table_name")

# Read a table back (like SELECT * FROM table)
spark.read.table("catalog.schema.table_name")

docs.title: What is a wildcard?
docs.text:
A wildcard is a stand-in character that means "anything can go here."

Think of it like a blank tile in Scrabble — it can represent anything. In data, you use a wildcard when you want to match a pattern rather than an exact value.

docs.title: You already know this: SQL LIKE
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'

The % is the wildcard. It means "I don't care what comes before @gmail.com — match anything."

Pattern Matches Doesn't match '%@gmail.com' john@gmail.com, x@gmail.com john@hotmail.com 'john%' john, johnny, johnson mr.john '%error%' critical_error_log, my_error_2 warning

There's also _ — exactly one character:

WHERE code LIKE 'A_C'   -- matches ABC, A1C, ACC — not AC, not ABBC

docs.title: Wildcards in PySpark: two places you'll use them
1. When reading files: load multiple files at once
docs.text:
# Load just one specific file
df = spark.read.csv("/Volumes/workspace/project/raw_files/sales_jan.csv")

# Load ALL csv files in the folder
df = spark.read.csv("/Volumes/workspace/project/raw_files/*.csv")

# Load only files that start with "sales_"
df = spark.read.csv("/Volumes/workspace/project/raw_files/sales_*.csv")

Think of it like selecting files in Windows Explorer — instead of Ctrl+clicking each one, you just say "give me everything ending in .csv."

Spark loads all matching files and combines them into one DataFrame automatically.

docs.title: 2. When filtering data: like() (same as SQL LIKE)
docs.text:
# SQL:     WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com'
# PySpark:
df.filter(df.email.like('%@gmail.com'))

# SQL:     WHERE status LIKE 'ERR%'
# PySpark:
df.filter(df.status.like('ERR%'))

Same logic as SQL — just written as a method on the column.

docs.title: Why this matters in real pipelines
docs.text:
Imagine Green Grid delivers a new meter readings file every day:

meter_readings_2024_01_01.json
meter_readings_2024_01_02.json
meter_readings_2024_01_03.json
... (365 files a year)

Without wildcards you'd write 365 separate read statements. With a wildcard:

df_readings = spark.read.json(
    "/Volumes/workspace/green_grid/raw_files/meter_readings_*.json",
    multiLine=True,
    schema=schema_readings
)

Spark finds every matching file and combines them all into one DataFrame. This is how production pipelines actually work — files land daily and the pipeline picks them all up without you changing any code.

docs.title: The SELECT * wildcard
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM table    -- * means "give me all columns"

# PySpark
df.select("*")
# In practice, display(df) already shows all columns

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Context Wildcard Meaning SQL LIKE % Zero or more of any character SQL LIKE _ Exactly one character PySpark like() % Same as SQL % PySpark like() _ Same as SQL _ File paths * Any file matching the pattern Column selection * All columns

docs.title: One thing to watch out for
docs.text:
When using * to load multiple files, all files must have the same structure — same columns, same types. If one file has an extra column or a different name, Spark will either error or fill missing columns with nulls.

This is another reason explicit schemas matter — when loading 365 files at once, you want Spark enforcing the structure, not guessing it from each file.

docs.title: Already familiar from SQL
docs.text:
AVG(Heart_Rate) OVER (PARTITION BY User_ID ORDER BY Timestamp)

PySpark's window functions work the same way. They look at rows related to the current row without collapsing them into one. That's what separates them from groupBy.

docs.title: The frozen sensor problem
docs.text:
A sensor freezes when it gets stuck sending the same heart rate over and over. SantéFlux had 150 frozen readings out of 750,000.

A working sensor moves. A frozen one flatlines. Detection: bucket readings into 10-minute windows per user. If min == max inside a bucket, the sensor didn't change. Those records skew the city averages and need to be removed before the report runs.

docs.title: Detecting frozen sensors
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, min, max, col

df_agg = df_hashed.groupBy(
    "hashed_id",
    window("Timestamp", "10 minutes")
).agg(
    min("Heart_Rate").alias("min_rate"),
    max("Heart_Rate").alias("max_rate")
)

# frozen windows
df_frozen = df_agg.filter(col("min_rate") == col("max_rate"))
df_frozen.count()

# clean data for reporting
df_clean = df_agg.filter(col("min_rate") != col("max_rate"))

window("Timestamp", "10 minutes") creates buckets: 08:00–08:10, 08:10–08:20, and so on. Same user, same bucket, same group. A frozen sensor — same reading ten times in a row — comes out with identical min and max.

docs.title: One gotcha — use window() directly in groupBy
docs.text:
window() creates a struct with start and end inside it. If you attach it with withColumn first and try to reference it by name in groupBy, Spark can't find it.

# Fails — CANNOT_RESOLVE_DATAFRAME_COLUMN
df = df.withColumn("tw", window("Timestamp", "10 minutes"))
df.groupBy("hashed_id", "tw")

# Works
df.groupBy("hashed_id", window("Timestamp", "10 minutes"))

Put window() directly in the groupBy. No intermediate column needed.

docs.title: groupBy vs window()
docs.text: groupBy window() Rows returned One per group Same count as input Collapses data? Yes No Use case Final aggregation (avg by city) Pattern detection (frozen per bucket)

docs.title: Where this fits in the pipeline
docs.text:
Raw ingest → mask names → hash + salt IDs → detect frozen sensors → aggregate → report

The frozen sensor check sits between hashing and final aggregation. Clean data only goes into the Health Trends Report.

See Hashing & Salting for why hashed_id is used instead of User_ID directly.

docs.title: 16. Delta Table Writes
docs.text:
Q: How do you write PySpark data to Delta tables?

30-sec answer

Use the DataFrame write API with format("delta"). You specify the write mode — append to add rows, overwrite to replace the table — and either a path or a table name registered in the metastore. Delta wraps the write in a transaction, so it's atomic and logged.

Deep dive

# Write to path
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/mnt/silver/transactions")

# Write to table (registers in metastore)
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("silver.transactions")

# With partitioning
df.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .partitionBy("event_date") \
    .save("/mnt/silver/events")

# Overwrite specific partitions only (dynamic partition overwrite)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/silver/events")

Write modes:

Mode Behaviour append Adds new files, never deletes existing data overwrite Replaces the entire table contents ignore Does nothing if table/path already exists error Raises error if table/path already exists (default)

What happens under the hood: 1. Spark writes new Parquet files to the Delta table directory 2. Delta logs the operation in the _delta_log/ transaction log (a JSON commit file) 3. The write is atomic — readers see either the full new data or the old data, never a partial state

Schema enforcement: Delta rejects writes where the incoming schema doesn't match the table schema. This catches pipeline bugs early instead of silently corrupting data.

# Enable schema evolution — add new columns from source automatically
df.write.format("delta") \
    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \
    .mode("append") \
    .save("/mnt/silver/transactions")

Follow-up: Why use Delta tables?

30-sec answer

Delta gives you three things standard Parquet doesn't: ACID transactions (writes are atomic, no partial reads), schema enforcement (bad data rejected at write time), and time travel (query any previous version with VERSION AS OF). For production pipelines these aren't nice-to-haves — they're what makes pipelines reliable.

docs.title: 17. MERGE Upserts
docs.text:
Q: How do you implement upserts in Delta?

30-sec answer

Use the Delta MERGE operation — it compares source and target data on a match condition, updates matching rows, inserts new ones, and optionally deletes rows that no longer exist in the source. It's the standard pattern for incremental pipeline loads.

Deep dive

from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forPath(spark, "/mnt/silver/customers")
source = spark.read.format("delta").load("/mnt/bronze/customers_new")

target.alias("target").merge(
    source.alias("source"),
    "target.customer_id = source.customer_id"
).whenMatchedUpdate(set={
    "name": "source.name",
    "email": "source.email",
    "updated_at": "source.updated_at"
}).whenNotMatchedInsert(values={
    "customer_id": "source.customer_id",
    "name": "source.name",
    "email": "source.email",
    "updated_at": "source.updated_at"
}).execute()

Full SCD Type 1 + delete pattern:

target.alias("target").merge(
    source.alias("source"),
    "target.customer_id = source.customer_id"
).whenMatchedUpdate(set={...})   # Update existing
.whenNotMatchedInsert(values={...})  # Insert new
.whenNotMatchedBySourceDelete()  # Delete removed records
.execute()

Performance considerations: - MERGE is expensive — it scans both source and target to find matches - Always filter source to only changed/new records before the MERGE - Partition the target table on a date or batch column so MERGE only touches relevant partitions - Use whenMatchedUpdateAll() and whenNotMatchedInsertAll() for brevity when column names align

CDC pattern (Change Data Capture): 

# Source has a 'operation' column: I=insert, U=update, D=delete
target.alias("t").merge(
    source.alias("s"),
    "t.id = s.id"
).whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.operation = 'D'") \
 .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.operation = 'U'") \
 .whenNotMatchedInsertAll(condition="s.operation = 'I'") \
 .execute()

Follow-up: Why is MERGE important?

30-sec answer

MERGE is what enables incremental pipelines — you only process new or changed data instead of reloading full tables on every run. It replaces the manual pattern of read-full-table, apply-changes, overwrite — which is both slow and risky. With MERGE, incremental loads are atomic and idempotent.

docs.title: 18. Delta Table Maintenance
docs.text:
Q: How do you maintain Delta tables?

30-sec answer

Two commands: OPTIMIZE for compacting small files into larger ones (targeting ~1GB), and VACUUM to physically delete data files no longer referenced by the transaction log. Without these, tables accumulate small files over time, which degrades query performance.

Deep dive

OPTIMIZE — file compaction:

-- Compact all files
OPTIMIZE silver.transactions

-- Compact + Z-order on frequently filtered columns
OPTIMIZE silver.transactions ZORDER BY (customer_id, event_date)

# Via PySpark
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
dt = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.transactions")
dt.optimize().executeCompaction()

When to run: after bulk appends, nightly after streaming pipelines, after MERGE operations that generate many small files.

VACUUM — removing obsolete files:

-- Remove files older than 7 days (default retention)
VACUUM silver.transactions

-- Shorter retention — be careful, disables time travel to that point
VACUUM silver.transactions RETAIN 168 HOURS

VACUUM and time travel

VACUUM permanently deletes old data files. After VACUUM, you cannot time travel to versions older than the retention period. Default is 7 days — don't reduce below your SLA for point-in-time recovery.

The small file problem in detail:

Every append write creates new Parquet files. A streaming pipeline appending every minute creates 1,440 files per day. After a month: 43,200 files. Spark has to open and read the footer of every single file during a scan — even if most files are filtered away by partition pruning. OPTIMIZE merges those into a handful of 1GB files.

Databricks managed OPTIMIZE: On Databricks, Auto Optimize and Auto Compaction can be enabled on tables: 

ALTER TABLE silver.transactions SET TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true',
  'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true'
)

Follow-up: Why is maintenance necessary?

30-sec answer

Without regular OPTIMIZE, append-heavy tables accumulate thousands of small files. Each file has overhead — Spark opens it, reads the footer, checks statistics. At scale, that metadata cost makes even simple queries slow. VACUUM clears dead files that are no longer in the transaction log, reclaiming storage and keeping the file listing lean.

docs.title: 19 & 20. File Size, Layout Optimisation & Data Skipping
docs.text:
These three concepts are tightly linked — covered together.

Q: What file size works best for Delta tables?

30-sec answer

Target 100MB to 1GB per file. Below 100MB and you start seeing metadata overhead dominate query time. Above 1GB and you reduce parallelism — fewer files means fewer tasks means fewer executors doing useful work in parallel.

Q: How do you optimise Delta table layout?

30-sec answer

Use Z-ordering to co-locate related data within files based on frequently filtered columns. On Microsoft Fabric, V-Order adds additional Parquet-level compression. Both techniques improve data skipping — Delta reads fewer files because related data is physically grouped together.

Q: What is data skipping?

30-sec answer

Delta stores min/max statistics for each column in each file. When a query has a filter, Delta checks those statistics and skips any files that can't contain matching rows — without opening them. Z-ordering makes data skipping more effective by ensuring similar values are in the same files.

Deep dive

File size and parallelism:

Spark assigns one task per file. If you have 5 executors and 5 files of 1GB each, all executors work simultaneously. If you have 5 executors and 500 files of 10MB each, Spark runs 100 rounds of 5 tasks — most time is spent in task scheduling overhead.

Ideal target: 

Total data size ÷ number of cores = target file size
(aim for ~200MB–1GB per file)

Z-ordering:

Z-order is a space-filling curve that interleaves multiple column values into a single ordering. This means rows with similar values in multiple columns end up in the same files — making multi-column filter queries extremely efficient.

OPTIMIZE silver.events ZORDER BY (customer_id, event_date)

Without Z-order: a filter on customer_id = 'X' AND event_date = '2025-01-15' might need to scan 500 files With Z-order: the same filter might touch only 3–4 files

V-Order (Microsoft Fabric specific):

V-Order is Fabric's proprietary Parquet optimisation — it applies additional sorting, dictionary encoding, and compression within each Parquet file. It's enabled by default in Fabric and makes reads faster without any code changes.

Data skipping in practice:

# Delta automatically collects stats on write
# Check stats with:
dt = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.events")
dt.detail().show()

# See how many files are being scanned vs skipped
spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.stats.skipping", "true")

When data skipping is most effective: - After Z-ordering on query predicates - On tables with good file size (not too small, not too large) - When filters are on columns with reasonable cardinality (not boolean columns)

Follow-up: Why is layout optimisation important?

30-sec answer

It's what makes Delta tables fast at query time. Without Z-ordering, data is laid out in the order it arrived — filters scan every file looking for matches. With Z-ordering on your most filtered columns, the same query touches a fraction of the files. On a 10TB table, that's the difference between a 2-minute scan and a 5-second one.

docs.title: 12. Spark Join Strategies
docs.text:
Q: What join strategies does Spark use?

30-sec answer

Spark has three main join strategies: broadcast join (small table copied to all executors, no shuffle), sort-merge join (both sides sorted and co-partitioned, used for large tables), and shuffle hash join (one side hashed in memory, cheaper than sort-merge but memory-intensive). Catalyst picks the strategy — but you can hint or force it.

Deep dive

1. Broadcast Hash Join

Best for: one small table + one large table

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

# Force broadcast — skips shuffle on large side entirely
result = df_large.join(broadcast(df_small), "customer_id")

How it works: - The small table is collected to the driver, then broadcast to every executor - Each executor holds the full small table in memory - The large table is scanned locally — no shuffle needed

Threshold: by default, tables under 10MB are auto-broadcast (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold — default 10MB, often worth raising to 100MB+)

2. Sort-Merge Join

Best for: two large tables

# Default for large tables — no hint needed
result = df_orders.join(df_customers, "customer_id")

How it works: - Both sides are shuffled and sorted by the join key - Executors merge-join their local sorted partitions - Expensive (two shuffles + two sorts) but works for any table size

3. Shuffle Hash Join

Best for: medium-sized tables where one side fits in executor memory

  • One side is hashed in memory, the other is streamed through
  • Cheaper than sort-merge (no sort step) but can OOM if hash table is too large
  • Usually enabled via spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin = false

Choosing the right strategy:

Situation Strategy One table < 100MB Broadcast hash join Both tables large, even distribution Sort-merge join Medium table, memory available Shuffle hash join Skewed keys Sort-merge + AQE skew handling

Join hints in PySpark:

# Broadcast hint
df_large.join(broadcast(df_lookup), "id")

# Merge hint (force sort-merge)
df_a.hint("merge").join(df_b, "id")

# Shuffle hash hint
df_a.hint("shuffle_hash").join(df_b, "id")

Common interview trap — Cartesian joins: If you join without a condition, Spark produces a Cartesian product — every row on the left matched with every row on the right. On large tables this is catastrophic. Always verify join conditions are correct before running in production.

Follow-up: When should broadcast joins be used?

30-sec answer

Use broadcast joins when one side of the join is small enough to fit in executor memory — typically lookup tables, dimension tables, or reference data. The threshold is configurable, but a good rule of thumb is anything under 100–200MB. Broadcasting eliminates the shuffle on the large side entirely, which is often the most expensive part of a join.

docs.title: 10. Partition Strategy
docs.text:
Q: How should tables be partitioned in lakehouse environments?

30-sec answer

Partition only on columns that are consistently used in filters — typically date fields like event_date or load_date. Avoid high-cardinality columns. In Delta tables specifically, over-partitioning creates a metadata problem that slows down reads more than it helps them.

Deep dive

Partitioning in Delta/Parquet means physically splitting data into separate folders based on column values:

/silver/events/event_date=2025-01-01/part-00001.parquet
/silver/events/event_date=2025-01-02/part-00001.parquet
...

When a query filters on event_date, Spark skips all non-matching folders entirely — this is partition pruning, and it's fast.

What goes wrong with bad partitioning:

Problem Cause Effect Too many partitions Partitioning on high-cardinality column (e.g., user_id) Millions of tiny files, slow metadata operations Too few partitions Only one or two distinct values (e.g., is_active) No benefit, large files per partition Wrong column Partitioning on a column rarely filtered No pruning benefit, just fragmentation

The small file problem: Each file has overhead — a Delta transaction log entry, file open/close cost, metadata in the Parquet footer. When you have millions of 1KB files, that metadata overhead dominates. A table with 10,000 x 1MB files is slower to query than one with 100 x 100MB files containing the same data.

Delta-specific guidance: - Date columns (day-level) work well for most event tables - Avoid partitioning on columns with more than ~10,000 distinct values - Use Z-ordering within partitions for further data skipping - Run OPTIMIZE after bulk loads to compact small files

Follow-up: What happens with excessive partitioning?

30-sec answer

Excessive partitioning creates two problems: metadata overhead and small files. Delta's transaction log has to track every file in every partition — with millions of partitions, even listing files becomes slow. And many small files mean Spark spawns thousands of tiny tasks, where task setup cost exceeds actual compute time.

docs.title: 11. Repartition vs Coalesce
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between repartition() and coalesce()?

30-sec answer

repartition(n) does a full shuffle to redistribute data evenly across n partitions — it can increase or decrease partition count. coalesce(n) only reduces partitions by merging them locally without a shuffle, making it cheaper but potentially leaving uneven partition sizes.

Deep dive

# Full shuffle — data redistributed evenly across 200 partitions
df_repart = df.repartition(200)

# No shuffle — merges existing partitions locally, reduces to 10
df_coalesce = df.coalesce(10)

# Repartition by column — ensures all rows with same key go to same partition
df_by_key = df.repartition(200, col("customer_id"))

When to use each:

Scenario Use Writing output files — want fewer, evenly-sized files coalesce() Before a join on a key column — align partitioning repartition(n, col) After a filter that dramatically reduced data size coalesce() Need guaranteed even distribution repartition() Need to increase partition count repartition() only — coalesce can't increase

The hidden cost of repartition(): It triggers a full shuffle — all data moves across the network. Use it deliberately. If you're just reducing partitions before a write, coalesce() is almost always the right choice.

Practical write pattern: 

# After heavy transformations, reduce to sensible file count before writing
df_final.coalesce(10).write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/gold/output")

Follow-up: When should coalesce() be used?

30-sec answer

Use coalesce() when reducing partitions before writing output files — it avoids an unnecessary shuffle. After filtering a large dataset down to a fraction of its original size, coalesce brings the partition count down without the cost of moving data across the network.

docs.title: 13. Shuffle Operations
docs.text:
Q: Why are shuffle operations expensive?

30-sec answer

A shuffle moves data between executors across the network so records with the same key end up on the same partition. This involves serialising data, writing shuffle files to disk, transferring them over the network, and reading them back. Each of those steps is orders of magnitude slower than in-memory computation.

Deep dive

What happens during a shuffle:

Stage 1 (map side):
  Each executor processes its partition
  → Sorts output records by target partition key
  → Writes shuffle files to local disk

Network transfer:
  Executors fetch the shuffle files they need from other executors

Stage 2 (reduce side):
  Each executor reads its portion of shuffle data
  → Deserialises and processes

Why disk I/O hits hard: Spark writes shuffle data to local executor disk before sending it. If executors run out of disk space, jobs fail. If disks are slow (spinning HDDs), shuffles become a bottleneck even before the network.

Operations that cause shuffles:

Operation Why it shuffles groupBy() + agg() All rows with same key must meet on one executor join() (sort-merge) Both sides sorted and co-partitioned by join key distinct() All copies of same value must be on one executor repartition() Explicit redistribution orderBy() Global sort requires all data on one executor then re-distributed

How to reduce shuffle cost: 1. Use broadcast joins when one side is small (eliminates shuffle on large side) 2. Filter and project before joins (less data to shuffle) 3. Pre-partition on join keys if joining repeatedly on the same key 4. Tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (default 200 — often wrong for your data size)

Follow-up: How do you minimise shuffles?

30-sec answer

Use broadcast joins for small tables — this eliminates the shuffle on the large side entirely. Pre-filter and project before any join to reduce the data volume being shuffled. Tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to match your actual data size — 200 is often too high for small datasets and too low for large ones.

docs.title: 15. Data Skew
docs.text:
Q: What is data skew?

30-sec answer

Data skew happens when data is unevenly distributed across partitions — typically because one key value appears far more often than others. One executor ends up processing 80% of the data while others sit idle, making the whole job wait for that one slow task to finish.

Deep dive

Classic skew scenario: you're joining a transactions table to a customers table on customer_id. One customer has 50 million transactions (a corporate account), while most have a few hundred. The partition holding that customer's key runs 100x longer than all others.

How to identify skew: - Spark UI: look for one task in a stage taking 10x longer than others - Stage timeline: all tasks finish quickly except one or two outliers - df.groupBy("key").count().orderBy(col("count").desc()).show() — spot dominant keys

Fix 1: Salting Add a random suffix to the skewed key to spread it across multiple partitions:

from pyspark.sql.functions import concat, col, lit, floor, rand

# Add salt to the large table
salt_factor = 10
df_large = df_large.withColumn("salted_key",
    concat(col("customer_id"), lit("_"), (floor(rand() * salt_factor)).cast("string")))

# Explode the small table to match all salt values
from pyspark.sql.functions import explode, array
df_small = df_small.withColumn("salt_range", array([lit(i) for i in range(salt_factor)]))
df_small = df_small.withColumn("salt", explode(col("salt_range")))
df_small = df_small.withColumn("salted_key",
    concat(col("customer_id"), lit("_"), col("salt").cast("string")))

# Now join on salted key
result = df_large.join(df_small, "salted_key").drop("salted_key", "salt", "salt_range")

Fix 2: AQE skew handling In Spark 3.x with AQE enabled, skewed partitions are automatically detected and split:

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor", "5")

Fix 3: Repartition before join 

df_large = df_large.repartition(200, col("customer_id"))

Follow-up: How do you fix data skew?

30-sec answer

Two main approaches: salting and AQE. Salting adds a random suffix to skewed keys, distributing one hot partition across many — you then explode the smaller side to match. AQE (enabled by default in Spark 3.2+) detects skewed partitions at runtime and splits them automatically. For known skew patterns, repartitioning on the join key before the join also helps.

docs.title: 23. Spark Caching Strategy
docs.text:
Q: When should caching be used?

30-sec answer

Cache when you reuse the same DataFrame multiple times in a pipeline and the computation to produce it is expensive. Don't cache raw source tables — Delta already handles file skipping and pushdown efficiently. Don't cache data you'll only use once. Cache intermediate aggregations or filtered datasets that feed multiple downstream steps.

Deep dive

Caching stores a DataFrame in executor memory (or memory + disk) so it doesn't need to be recomputed on each action.

# Without cache — df_filtered is computed twice
df_filtered = df.filter(col("status") == "active").join(df_lookup, "id")
count = df_filtered.count()           # Spark runs the full pipeline
summary = df_filtered.groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount"))  # Runs again

# With cache — computed once, reused
df_filtered.cache()
df_filtered.count()      # First action triggers computation and caches result
summary = df_filtered.groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount"))  # Read from cache

# Always unpersist when done
df_filtered.unpersist()

Cache storage levels:

from pyspark import StorageLevel

df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY)           # Fastest, drops if OOM
df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)       # Spills to disk if OOM (safer)
df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)             # Slow, use only for very large data
df.cache()                                      # Shortcut for MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER

What not to cache:

Don't cache Why Raw Delta tables Delta's data skipping + pushdown is already efficient DataFrames used only once Caching has overhead — wastes memory Streaming DataFrames Not supported in the same way Very large DataFrames Risk of OOM or excessive GC pressure

Signs you need caching: - The same DataFrame appears in multiple branches of your pipeline - Spark UI shows the same stage running twice with identical plans - Job has iterative computation (loops, graph algorithms)

Follow-up: What should not be cached?

30-sec answer

Raw Delta tables — they already benefit from file skipping, column pruning, and predicate pushdown at the storage layer, so caching them just wastes executor memory. Also avoid caching DataFrames you only read once — the overhead of writing to cache storage isn't worth it for single-use data.

docs.title: 24. Spark Checkpointing
docs.text:
Q: What is checkpointing?

30-sec answer

Checkpointing saves a DataFrame's computed state to durable storage, breaking the lineage chain. Unlike caching (which is memory-based and lost on failure), checkpoints are written to a reliable filesystem and survive executor failures or context resets.

Deep dive

Every transformation adds a node to the RDD lineage graph. In long-running or iterative jobs, that lineage can become extremely long:

read → filter → join → groupBy → window → join → groupBy → join → ...

If any step fails, Spark recomputes the entire lineage from scratch. Checkpointing truncates that chain:

# Set checkpoint directory (persistent storage)
spark.sparkContext.setCheckpointDir("/mnt/checkpoints/job_xyz")

# Checkpoint a DataFrame — writes to disk and breaks lineage
df_intermediate.checkpoint()

# Truncated lineage — recovery only goes back to checkpoint, not original source

Checkpoint vs Cache:

Cache Checkpoint Storage Executor memory/disk Durable filesystem (HDFS, ADLS, S3) Lineage Preserved Truncated Fault tolerant No (lost on executor failure) Yes Use case Reuse within a session Long lineage, iterative jobs, streaming

Structured Streaming checkpoints:

In streaming, checkpoints are mandatory — they store the stream's current offset and state:

df_stream.writeStream \
    .format("delta") \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/stream_xyz") \
    .start("/mnt/silver/events")

Without a checkpoint, a streaming job that restarts loses track of where it was in the source and reprocesses data.

Follow-up: When is checkpointing used?

30-sec answer

Two main scenarios: streaming pipelines (mandatory — stores offset and state so restarts resume where they left off) and iterative batch computations like graph algorithms or ML training loops where lineage grows very long. In iterative jobs, checkpointing every few iterations prevents Spark from needing to replay the full history on failure.

docs.title: 25. Spark Debugging
docs.text:
Q: How do you debug slow Spark jobs?

30-sec answer

Start with the Spark UI — look at the Stages tab for tasks that are taking disproportionately long, the SQL tab for the physical execution plan, and the Executors tab for GC pressure or memory issues. Most slow jobs fall into three categories: data skew, large shuffles, or insufficient partitioning.

Deep dive

Step-by-step debug approach:

1. Check the Spark UI — Stages tab - Are all tasks in a stage completing at similar times, or is one task running 10x longer? → Data skew - Are there many stages? → Too many shuffles - Is shuffle read/write size very large? → Reduce data volume before shuffle

2. Check the SQL tab — physical plan 

df.explain(True)  # Shows logical + physical plan
df.explain("formatted")  # Cleaner output in Spark 3.x
Look for: - Exchange nodes → shuffle operations - BroadcastExchange → broadcast join (good for small tables) - SortMergeJoin → expensive, check if broadcast is possible - Filter pushed below Scan → predicate pushdown working

3. Check the Executors tab - High GC time (>10% of task time) → memory pressure, tune executor memory or reduce data - Some executors doing much more work than others → skew

Common root causes and fixes:

Symptom Root cause Fix One task takes 100x longer Data skew Salting, AQE skew join Many small stages Too many shuffles Reduce groupBy/join operations, pre-partition OOM errors Executor memory too small or cache overuse Tune spark.executor.memory, reduce cache Long GC pauses Too many objects in JVM heap Use Tungsten off-heap, increase memory Job takes forever but tasks are fast Driver bottleneck from .collect() Avoid collecting large datasets to driver

Quick diagnostic code:

# Check partition sizes
df.rdd.mapPartitionsWithIndex(lambda i, it: [(i, sum(1 for _ in it))]).collect()

# Check data distribution on a key
df.groupBy("customer_id").count().orderBy(col("count").desc()).show(20)

# Time a specific operation
import time
start = time.time()
df.count()
print(f"Elapsed: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

Follow-up: Most common cause of slow jobs?

30-sec answer

Data skew and large shuffle operations — they account for the majority of slow job complaints in production. Data skew means one task does the work of a hundred others, making the whole stage wait. Large shuffles mean massive disk I/O and network transfer between stages. Both are visible in the Spark UI within minutes of investigation.

docs.title: 6. Catalyst Optimizer
docs.text:
Q: What does the Catalyst optimizer do?

30-sec answer

Catalyst is Spark's query optimisation engine. It takes your logical query plan — what you wrote in PySpark — and rewrites it into the most efficient physical execution plan before any data is read. It applies rules like pushing filters closer to the source, eliminating unnecessary columns, and selecting the best join strategy.

Deep dive

Catalyst works in four phases:

1. Analysis       → Resolves column names, table references, data types
2. Logical Opt    → Applies rule-based optimisations (predicate pushdown, projection pruning)
3. Physical Plan  → Generates multiple physical plans, picks the cheapest via cost model
4. Code Gen       → Compiles the plan to JVM bytecode (via Tungsten whole-stage codegen)

Key optimisations Catalyst applies automatically:

Optimisation What it does Predicate pushdown Moves filter() as close to storage as possible Projection pruning Reads only columns you actually use Constant folding Evaluates constant expressions at compile time Join reordering Puts smaller tables on the broadcast side Null propagation Simplifies null comparisons in expressions

Practical example:

# You write this
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/silver/sales")
result = df.select("region", "amount").filter(col("region") == "EMEA").groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount"))

Catalyst rewrites the execution order to: 1. Read only region and amount columns (projection pruning) 2. Filter rows where region == "EMEA" at scan time (predicate pushdown) 3. Then group and aggregate

The code you wrote is logically correct but not execution-ordered — Catalyst fixes that for you.

Follow-up: Examples of Catalyst optimisations?

30-sec answer

The three most impactful: predicate pushdown (filters applied at the storage layer before data is read), projection pruning (only requested columns are scanned), and join reordering (smaller datasets are placed on the broadcast side to avoid expensive sort-merge joins).

docs.title: 7. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
docs.text:
Q: What is Adaptive Query Execution?

30-sec answer

AQE is a runtime optimisation system introduced in Spark 3.0. Unlike Catalyst, which optimises before execution, AQE monitors what actually happens during a query and adjusts the plan mid-flight — changing join strategies, merging small shuffle partitions, and handling skewed data automatically.

Deep dive

Catalyst optimises based on statistics collected before execution. Those statistics can be wrong — especially for data with skew, after joins, or when stats haven't been refreshed. AQE fixes this by making decisions based on real runtime data.

Three main AQE features:
