1. Dynamic coalescing of shuffle partitions After a shuffle, AQE checks the actual output partition sizes. If many partitions are tiny, it merges them before the next stage — avoiding thousands of small tasks.

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")

2. Dynamic switching of join strategies If a table was estimated to be large but turns out small at runtime, AQE switches from a sort-merge join to a broadcast join on the fly.

3. Dynamic skew join optimisation If one partition is 5x larger than the median, AQE splits that partition and processes it separately — preventing one slow task from blocking the entire stage.

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")

AQE is enabled by default in Spark 3.2+ — but knowing it exists helps you diagnose cases where it's not firing as expected.

Follow-up: What problems does AQE solve?

30-sec answer

AQE specifically targets two common production problems: data skew (where one partition holds far more data than others, slowing the whole job) and inefficient shuffle partitions (where the default 200 partitions creates either too many small tasks or too few large ones). It handles both dynamically at runtime.

docs.title: 8. Predicate Pushdown
docs.text:
Q: What is predicate pushdown?

30-sec answer

Predicate pushdown moves filter conditions as close to the data source as possible — ideally to the storage layer — so Spark reads only the rows it needs. Instead of loading a full table and filtering in memory, the filter is applied during the file scan itself.

Deep dive

Without predicate pushdown: 

Read 500GB table into Spark memory → filter 490GB away → process 10GB

With predicate pushdown: 

Storage layer reads only matching rows → Spark receives 10GB → process 10GB

How it works with Delta / Parquet:

Delta and Parquet files store column statistics (min, max, null count) at the file level. When Catalyst pushes a predicate like date >= '2025-01-01', it checks those stats and skips entire files that can't contain matching rows — without reading them at all.

# Predicate pushdown fires here — Delta skips non-matching files at scan time
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/silver/events") \
    .filter(col("event_date") >= "2025-01-01") \
    .filter(col("region") == "UK")

When predicate pushdown doesn't fire: - Filters applied after a join or aggregation (no longer at source) - Using UDFs in filter conditions (Catalyst can't translate them to storage predicates) - Complex expressions that can't be serialised to the storage format

Tip: Run df.explain(True) and look for PushedFilters in the physical plan output to confirm pushdown is happening.

Follow-up: Why is it important?

30-sec answer

It reduces I/O — the most expensive operation in distributed systems. Reading less data from storage means less network transfer, less memory pressure, and faster queries. On large Delta tables the difference between a scan of 1TB vs 10GB can be the difference between a 2-minute query and a 20-minute one.

docs.title: 9. Projection Pruning
docs.text:
Q: What is projection pruning?

30-sec answer

Projection pruning means Spark reads only the columns your query actually needs. If your table has 50 columns but your query uses 3, Spark and the underlying storage layer (Parquet/Delta) will skip the other 47 entirely — at the file level, before data reaches executors.

Deep dive

Parquet (the underlying format for Delta) is columnar — each column is stored separately on disk. This means skipping a column is a genuine I/O saving, not just filtering in memory.

# Spark reads ALL 50 columns — wasteful
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/silver/customers")
result = df.select("customer_id", "country", "signup_date")

# Catalyst sees only 3 columns are needed and prunes the rest at scan time

Why SELECT * is dangerous in Spark: It disables projection pruning. Every column gets read, even ones you never use. On wide tables with many columns (audit fields, metadata, nested structs), this adds significant I/O cost.

Projection pruning + predicate pushdown together:

These two optimisations combine to make Delta table scans extremely efficient: - Predicate pushdown skips rows (entire files or row groups) - Projection pruning skips columns

Used together on a 1TB table, you might end up reading only a few GB of relevant data.

Follow-up: Why is it beneficial?

30-sec answer

It reduces both disk I/O and memory usage. In columnar formats like Parquet and Delta, columns not needed are simply not read from disk. On wide tables — 30, 50, 100 columns — this can cut scan time and memory footprint dramatically, especially when queries only need 3–5 columns.

docs.title: 1. Role of PySpark in Lakehouse Platforms
docs.text:
Q: Where does PySpark fit in modern lakehouse architectures?

30-sec answer

PySpark is the distributed processing engine at the core of lakehouse platforms like Databricks and Microsoft Fabric. It handles large-scale transformations on data stored in Delta tables — powering ETL pipelines, feature engineering, streaming, and analytical workloads. It sits between raw storage and the consumption layer.

Deep dive

A lakehouse combines the flexibility of a data lake with the reliability of a data warehouse. PySpark is what makes the "processing" layer of that architecture work at scale.

In practice, the flow looks like this:

Raw files (Parquet / CSV / JSON in OneLake or S3)
        ↓
    PySpark transforms (clean, join, aggregate)
        ↓
    Delta tables (Bronze → Silver → Gold)
        ↓
    BI / ML / Analytics consumers

PySpark abstracts the complexity of distributed computing — you write Python DataFrame code, and Spark distributes execution across a cluster automatically. On Databricks, this is backed by the Photon engine. On Fabric, it runs on managed Spark pools against OneLake.

Why not just use SQL for everything? SQL is great for querying, but complex transformations — schema evolution, conditional logic, looping over datasets, ML feature pipelines — need a programmatic engine. PySpark gives you that without leaving the distributed execution model.

Follow-up: Why is PySpark preferred for large-scale ETL?

30-sec answer

Spark splits data into partitions and processes them in parallel across executor nodes. A transformation that would take hours on a single machine runs in minutes when distributed. It also optimises execution automatically through the Catalyst query planner — so you don't need to hand-tune every query.

docs.title: 2. DataFrame API vs RDD
docs.text:
Q: Why is the DataFrame API preferred over RDD?

30-sec answer

DataFrames sit on top of Spark's Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine. This means Spark can automatically reorder operations, push filters down to storage, and generate efficient bytecode at runtime. RDDs have none of that — every operation runs exactly as written, with no automatic optimisation.

Deep dive

RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets) were the original Spark abstraction. They're powerful but low-level — you manage partitioning, serialisation, and execution logic yourself.

DataFrames add a structured schema layer on top, which unlocks:

Feature RDD DataFrame Catalyst optimisation No Yes Tungsten memory management No Yes Predicate pushdown No Yes Python → JVM overhead High Low (Tungsten bypasses JVM for columnar ops) Readable code Verbose Concise

In production, DataFrames are almost always the right choice. The Catalyst optimizer builds a logical plan from your code, optimises it (reordering filters, pruning columns, choosing join strategies), and compiles it to an efficient physical plan before execution.

When RDD still makes sense: - You need fine-grained control over partitioning logic - Working with unstructured data that has no schema - Custom serialisation requirements - Iterative ML algorithms that need direct partition manipulation

Follow-up: When would you use RDD instead?

30-sec answer

Only when you need low-level control that the DataFrame API can't provide — such as custom partition logic, unstructured data without a fixed schema, or operations that require direct access to individual records without schema inference.

docs.title: 3. Lazy Evaluation
docs.text:
Q: What is lazy evaluation in Spark?

30-sec answer

Spark does not execute transformations when you write them. Instead, it records each operation in a logical plan and waits. When an action is triggered — like count() or write() — Spark compiles the full plan, optimises it, and only then runs computation across the cluster.

Deep dive

Lazy evaluation is one of the most important design decisions in Spark. It lets Spark see the full picture of what you want to do before deciding how to do it.

Example — without lazy evaluation, this would scan the full table three times:

df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/data/orders")
df_filtered = df.filter(col("country") == "UK")
df_renamed = df_filtered.withColumnRenamed("order_id", "id")
df_final = df_renamed.select("id", "amount")

With lazy evaluation, Spark sees all four steps together. Before execution it: 1. Pushes the filter down to storage (only reads UK rows) 2. Prunes columns (only reads order_id and amount) 3. Combines all steps into a single scan pass

The result: one efficient scan instead of four.

The DAG connection

Each transformation adds a node to the DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph). When an action fires, Spark submits the full DAG to the scheduler, which breaks it into stages and tasks.

Follow-up: What triggers execution?

30-sec answer

Actions trigger execution. Common ones: count(), collect(), show(), write(), first(), take(n), save(). Transformations like filter(), select(), join() never trigger execution on their own — they only build the plan.

docs.title: 4. Transformations vs Actions
docs.text:
Q: What is the difference between transformations and actions?

30-sec answer

Transformations build the execution plan — they're lazy and return a new DataFrame without running anything. Actions trigger actual computation and either return a result to the driver or write data to storage. This split is what enables Spark's query optimisation.

Deep dive

Type Behaviour Examples Narrow transformation No shuffle, each partition maps to one output partition filter(), select(), withColumn(), map() Wide transformation Requires shuffle across partitions groupBy(), join(), distinct(), orderBy() Action Triggers execution, returns result count(), collect(), show(), write(), first()

Why the distinction matters in production:

Wide transformations (shuffle operations) are the expensive ones — data has to move across the network between executors. Every groupBy() or join() on unpartitioned data causes a full shuffle. Knowing this helps you design pipelines that minimise data movement.

# This builds a plan — nothing runs yet
df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/silver/transactions")
df_agg = df.filter(col("status") == "completed").groupBy("customer_id").agg(sum("amount"))

# This triggers execution — everything above runs now
df_agg.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/gold/customer_spend")

Follow-up: Example?

30-sec answer

select(), filter(), withColumn(), join() are all transformations — they return DataFrames and add nodes to the plan. count(), collect(), show(), and write() are actions — they submit the plan for execution and return a result.

docs.title: 5. Spark DAG Execution Model
docs.text:
Q: How does Spark execute jobs internally?

30-sec answer

When an action is triggered, Spark converts the transformation chain into a DAG — a directed acyclic graph of operations. The DAG Scheduler breaks this into stages at shuffle boundaries. Each stage is divided into tasks, one per partition, and those tasks run in parallel across executor nodes.

Deep dive

The execution flow from code to result:

Your PySpark code
      ↓
  Logical Plan (Catalyst parses and validates)
      ↓
  Optimised Logical Plan (Catalyst applies rules: pushdown, pruning)
      ↓
  Physical Plan (Catalyst selects join strategy, scan method)
      ↓
  DAG of RDD operations
      ↓
  DAG Scheduler → splits into Stages at shuffle boundaries
      ↓
  Task Scheduler → assigns Tasks (one per partition) to Executors
      ↓
  Executors run tasks in parallel

Stages and tasks: - A stage is a group of tasks that can run without a shuffle - A task processes one partition - Stage boundaries are always shuffle operations (groupBy, join, repartition)

Why this matters: If you see a query that has many stages in the Spark UI, each stage boundary is a shuffle. Each shuffle writes data to disk and reads it back — that's where most job time is spent. Reducing stage count = reducing shuffles = faster jobs.

Follow-up: What determines stage boundaries?

30-sec answer

Shuffle operations determine stage boundaries. Any operation that requires data to move between partitions — groupBy(), join(), distinct(), repartition() — creates a new stage. Within a stage, all tasks run independently without any data exchange.

docs.title: 14. Window Functions
docs.text:
Q: When are window functions used?

30-sec answer

Window functions compute values across a set of rows related to the current row — without collapsing them into a single result like groupBy does. Use them for rankings, running totals, moving averages, deduplication, and comparing a row to its neighbours. They're one of the most powerful tools in PySpark for analytical transformations.

Deep dive

The key distinction from groupBy: window functions return a value per row, not per group.

from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number, rank, dense_rank, lag, lead, sum, avg
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Define a window spec — partition + ordering
window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("transaction_date")

Common window function patterns:

1. Deduplication — keep latest record per key

window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(col("updated_at").desc())

df_deduped = df.withColumn("rn", row_number().over(window)) \
               .filter(col("rn") == 1) \
               .drop("rn")

2. Running total

window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("transaction_date") \
               .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

df = df.withColumn("running_total", sum("amount").over(window))

3. Ranking within group

window = Window.partitionBy("region").orderBy(col("revenue").desc())

df = df.withColumn("rank", rank().over(window)) \
       .withColumn("dense_rank", dense_rank().over(window))

4. Lag / Lead — compare to previous or next row

window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("transaction_date")

df = df.withColumn("prev_amount", lag("amount", 1).over(window)) \
       .withColumn("next_amount", lead("amount", 1).over(window)) \
       .withColumn("change", col("amount") - col("prev_amount"))

5. Moving average

# 7-day rolling average
window = Window.partitionBy("product_id").orderBy("date") \
               .rowsBetween(-6, 0)  # Current row + 6 preceding

df = df.withColumn("7d_avg", avg("sales").over(window))

rank() vs dense_rank() vs row_number():

Function Ties behaviour Gaps in sequence row_number() Arbitrary order for ties No gaps — always 1,2,3,4 rank() Same rank for ties Gaps after ties — 1,1,3,4 dense_rank() Same rank for ties No gaps — 1,1,2,3

Performance note: Window functions trigger a shuffle — data must be co-located by partitionBy key before the window can compute. For large datasets, make sure your partitionBy column aligns with your physical partitioning to avoid unnecessary data movement.

Follow-up: Example of window function use?

30-sec answer

The most common production use is deduplication: use row_number() over a window partitioned by the entity key and ordered by a timestamp descending, then filter to row number 1. This gives you the latest version of each record. It's cleaner and more efficient than a self-join or a groupBy + re-join pattern.
